newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BONN STRIKES TAX DEAL TO STIMULATE GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BONN STRIKES TAX DEAL TO STIMULATE GROWTH.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition on Wednesday struck a deal to cut income taxes in a major reform the government hopes will help tackle the country's most urgent problem -- the need to put four million jobless back to work.

Speaking as he entered a marathon final meeting of a tax working group, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the new rates would create "a real incentive for new jobs" in an economy that has yet to deliver on higher growth expectations.

Waigel did not give details, but sources from the policy group said a compromise model had been agreed between Waigel's wish to keep Germany's sliding tax scale and the call by junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP) for a low entry rate.

The new tax model would start with a flat rate of 15 percent on annual income of between 13,000 and 20,000 marks. The rate would then jump to 22 percent and rise in a straight line to a top rate of 39 percent.
The new tax model -- which is expected to be introduced in 1999 -- would cut income taxes sharply from today's entry rate of 26 percent and top rate of 53 percent.
The progress on a tax deal came as a Reuters survey of 38 European economists on Wednesday forecast the German economy would grow 2.2 percent in 1997, up from 1.4 percent last year.
The average forecast was only slightly below the government's own expectations.
According to Bonn's annual economic report, obtained by Reuters and not due to be released until January 28, the German economy should grow 2.5 percent during 1997.
But the tax deal and optimistic economic outlook have not eased concern in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's re-election camp.
Bold tax cut proposals, to be unveiled today, were conceived as a popular step similar to, but not as radical, as the U.S. and British supply-side policies introduced in the 1980s.
But political wrangling, soured by talk of raising VAT and other taxes to recoup lost revenues, appear to have watered down the good news Bonn wanted to announce ahead of 1998's elections.

Indeed, economic growth is expected to do little to shorten Germany's record long unemployment lines, getting people off benefit lists and paying taxes which could be used to slash deficits towards entry-level targets for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
With the jobless rate at 10.3 percent last year, the Economics Ministry forecast unemployment could climb to 11 percent while private economists see the rate at 10.7 percent.
Germany's Bundesbank will have a chance to help boost employment at its regular council meeting on Thursday, but the economists surveyed by Reuters saw little room for it to lower interest rates.
The economists said long-term and official interest rates have now bottomed and will start to head higher this year, with the Bundesbank likely to raise rates at the turn of the year.

Maybe more important than interest rates for the economy is the direction of the dollar. Economists said that the weaker German currency is helping German exporters, shoring up on of the key pillars of the economy.
The dollar was on Wednesday trading around 1.64 marks, its highest level since June 1994 and some 13 percent up on last year's low of 1.45 marks.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said that the dollar's strength would not "import" inflation to Germany and that the German currency could not continue to depreciate against the dollar at the pace seen over the last few days.
Economists polled by Reuters said they see the mark languishing through the middle of 1997 before steadily recovering against the U.S. currency ahead of the planned 1999 start of the euro.
